rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: FPSO and FSU dutyholders must regularly monitor cargo and slop-tank ullage spaces for toxic gases such as hydrogen sulphide.

rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: Monitoring must use appropriate equipment even when process trains do not indicate high hydrogen-sulphide concentrations.

rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: Detected hydrogen sulphide requires an implemented management process consistent with relevant offshore guidance.

rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: Major-accident hazard reviews must identify, evaluate and control high-concentration toxic-gas exposure scenarios.

rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: Fixed gas monitoring can reduce the need to expose personnel using portable equipment.

rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: Venting controls may need restrictions on personnel presence and minimum wind conditions.

rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: Preventive measures can include dewatering, biociding and maintenance of tank-stripping systems.

rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: COSHH, offshore safety-case, PFEER and integrity duties can all be relevant to hydrogen-sulphide control.

rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: Offshore hydrogen-sulphide risk depends on concentration, tank conditions, biological activity, venting, wind, monitoring, maintenance and worker location.

rows.source: HSE offshore hydrogen-sulphide monitoring and control
rows.verified: Offshore H2S evidence is installation-, tank-, concentration-, weather-, task- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level toxic-exposure probability.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: DSEAR covers dangerous substances, ATEX and explosive atmospheres, petrol storage, acetylene and work-process fire safety.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: Dangerous substances include flammable gases, liquids and solids as well as substances that can generate explosive atmospheres.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: Flashpoint is the minimum test temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to ignite momentarily.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: Uncontrolled releases from pressurised flammable-gas containers can ignite or turn cylinders into missiles.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: Fuel gases and oxygen used for hot work can create fire and explosion risks without other dangerous substances.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: HSE provides resources for controlling fire and explosion risks across construction, oxygen use, gas detection and dangerous substances.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: HSE fire-and-explosion guidance covers workplace controls, oxygen use, pentane, explosive materials and flammable-gas detection.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: Dutyholders must apply the relevant dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere requirements to the substances and work processes present.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: DSEAR risk depends on substance properties, inventory, process, containment, release frequency, ventilation, ignition sources, occupancy and emergency arrangements.

rows.source: HSE dangerous-substance and explosive-atmosphere controls
rows.verified: Dangerous-substance evidence is substance-, process-, installation-, environment- and scenario-specific and is not an exact parcel-level incident probability.
